plan.title: AI Model Releases of Late 2026: What Actually Mattered
plan.description: A look at the biggest AI model releases from October and November 2026, including GPT-6.2, Gemini 4 and Claude Fable 5.2. It explains the trends behind them: tiered model families, fast-changing leaderboards, and the push toward open weights and model choice.

beats.narration: Which AI model is the best in the world? On October 27, the answer was Claude Opus 5.5. Just one day later, that answer was wrong. Here is how fast the frontier really moves.

props.title: The leaderboard that flipped in one day
props.subtitle: AI frontier models, late October to mid-November 2026

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.chapter: A leaderboard that flipped in one day

beats.narration: On October 27, Artificial Analysis launched Intelligence Index version 5, a benchmark that scores AI models. Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 took first place on the very first day.

props.definition: A benchmark from Artificial Analysis that scores AI models. Launched October 27, 2026, with Claude Opus 5.5 in first place.

beats.narration: One day later, Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon. It took first place with a score of 59. Claude Opus 5.5 slipped to second at 58, and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra sat third at 57.
But Carbon began with a tiny audience. Google first gave it only to a small group of cyber defenders, and then widened access slowly through its Fairwind Program.

Then the releases came fast. On November 9, Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.2. On November 10, Gemini 4 Carbon reached paying developers and enterprises, at an introductory price of two dollars per million input tokens.
Consumers get Carbon in phases. Google AI Ultra subscribers came first. Then on November 16, Google AI Pro subscribers got it in AI Mode. Not everyone has it yet.

steps.label: Google AI Pro in AI Mode

beats.narration: So here is the lesson. Any claim that a model is the best needs a date and a source, because the top spot can change within a day.

props.text: Every best-model claim needs a date and a source.

beats.narration: Labs no longer ship one model. They ship a family. Google's Gemini 4 has Hydrogen for everyday speed, Neon in the middle, and Carbon for the hardest work.
beats.chapter: Model families: big, fast and cheap tiers

beats.narration: Hydrogen arrived on November 12, and free users get it too. Pricing is counted in tokens, which are small chunks of text, roughly a word or part of one.

props.definition: A small chunk of text, roughly a word or part of one. AI models read and bill in tokens.
props.example: Prices are quoted per million tokens.

beats.narration: Then came Neon on November 18. It costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. It has a one million token context window, and it replaced Argon.
The context window is how much text a model can hold in mind at once. And cached input on Neon costs just fifteen cents per million, a 95 percent discount.

props.label: Discount on cached input: $0.15 per million tokens

beats.narration: OpenAI did the same on November 17, in ChatGPT Work, Codex and the API. GPT-6.2 Astra costs $8 input and $40 output. Sol costs $2 input and $10 output.
Here's the math. Astra output is $40 per million tokens. Sol output is $10. That is a four times gap, so picking the right tier decides your bill.
Not every strong model sits behind an API. Open weights let anyone download the model and run it. Moonshot promised full weights for Kimi K3.1 Pro by November 4.

props.text: Open weights: download it, run it, no permission needed.

beats.chapter: Open weights, choice and what to watch

beats.narration: Then came Inkling 2 Mini, Apache 2.0, on November 20. It runs on a laptop. Two days later, on November 22, Sarvam-105B-1711 joined the open-weight list.
The frontier is not only American. Alibaba's Qwen4-Max arrived on November 16. Microsoft's MAI Code 2 followed on November 17, a coding specialist built in-house.
Also at Ignite on November 17, business Copilot let users choose OpenAI or Anthropic models. The buyer now picks the engine, not just the vendor.
The pace is hard to overstate. According to BeevR, 27 model releases from 13 vendors were confirmed between November 1 and 24.
So the takeaway is simple. No single model wins. Match the model to the job, whether that is coding, writing or budget work. And check the date on any ranking.

accuracy.reason: Most figures match the notes, but several claims are shaky or contradictory. Carbon's Oct 28 announcement is described as 'tiny audience... cyber defenders', and Kimi K3.1 Pro weights are stated as released on Nov 4 though the notes only say 'promised'. The Neon cached-price math is also loosely framed.

coverage.reason: It covers Google, OpenAI and Anthropic releases, pricing, open weights and Qwen/Microsoft. It says almost nothing about capabilities, agents, reasoning trends or caveats. Claude Fable 5.2 gets one line and nothing on what it does.

structure.reason: The three chapters are clear, but the first runs long on one leaderboard story. The timeline in beat 5 is titled 'November' yet starts in October. Beats 9-11 mix tokens, Hydrogen, Neon and the context window awkwardly.

hook_ending.reason: The hook 'On October 27, the answer was Claude Opus 5.5. Just one day later, that answer was wrong' creates tension. The ending is a plain three-bullet recap, which is serviceable but not memorable.

tone.reason: Plain, clear, beginner-friendly explainer voice appropriate for a US general audience.

visuals.reason: Scene types vary well, and the chart and table use real numbers. The gallery uses generic queries like 'programmer writing code monitor', and the Nov 4 open-weights timeline entry is shaky.

originality.reason: The one-day leaderboard flip is a concrete, memorable detail. The rest is a list of dates and prices, and the 'date and source' lesson is repeated.

instructions.reason: It is in English and roughly on length. It addresses 'releases and trends' but is thin on trends (agents, reasoning, cost) and leans on a list of releases.

language.reason: Fluent, clean sentences. A few clipped lines and the 'Here's the math' phrasing are minor.
